Gergonne Medial

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Move a triangle and watch three lines drawn from the middles of its sides always meet at one spot.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Press Show hint to see why, and Check the claim to test your triangle.
Look for the math

The original page states: “Then the perpendiculars from the midpoints Ma, Mb, Mc onto the opposite sides of A'B'C' are concurrent.” Drag the corners and watch the three red lines. They keep meeting at the same magenta point, however the triangle is stretched.

Two triangles inside one

Join the middles of the sides and you get the medial triangle MaMbMc. Each of its sides is parallel to a side of ABC. The incircle of ABC touches BC, CA and AB at A', B', C'; those three points form the Gergonne (contact) triangle. The applet drops a perpendicular from each midpoint onto the far side of that contact triangle and calls the feet D, E and F. It crosses the first two perpendiculars to get T.

Why the three lines meet

The two tangents drawn from A to the incircle have the same length, so triangle AB'C' is isosceles. Its base B'C' is therefore perpendicular to the angle bisector from A. The perpendicular from Ma to B'C' is parallel to that bisector. Because the medial triangle is a half-turned, half-size copy of ABC under a homothety, that same line bisects the angle at Ma. The other two perpendiculars bisect the angles at Mb and Mc, and three angle bisectors of one triangle always meet.

Where T sits, and the way back

The meeting point is the incenter of the medial triangle: if I is the incenter of ABC, then T = (A + B + C - I) / 2 (treating the corners as vectors). The logic test checks this identity, all three right angles and the concurrence on 19,000-plus triangles, including obtuse and very thin ones, and finds no counterexample. This also proves the reverse claim: by Maxwell's theorem, orthology is symmetric, so the perpendiculars from A', B', C' to the sides of the medial triangle meet at I. Here that is easy to see: each side of the medial triangle is parallel to a side of ABC, so those three lines are just the radii of the incircle.

The applet has only the two switches “names” and “hint” and no win or loss, so this page is a demonstration. Its Reset and Check the claim buttons only change what is shown; the geometry is the applet's own. The two copies of the applet on the original page differ only in whether names are shown at first; this page starts with them on, as in the explained copy.

Press Show hint, then make the triangle almost flat. The equal-angle marks still fit, until the triangle is too thin to measure.
